nameStory: The 'threelobe' in this spirea's name comes from its distinctive leaves, which are divided into three rounded lobes that look like a three-fingered mitten. The word 'spirea' comes from the Greek word 'speira,' meaning wreath, referring to how these shrubs' flexible branches were once twisted into garlands and wreaths.
description: Threelobe Spirea is a graceful deciduous shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall and wide. It's originally from Asia but has occasionally escaped cultivation in North America. This member of the rose family produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring and has distinctive three-lobed leaves that give it its common name. It's quite rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The key identifying feature: leaves are divided into three distinct rounded lobes, feeling smooth to the touch with a slightly glossy surface and serrated edges on each lobe

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with five petals arranged in flat-topped or slightly rounded clusters, each flower about 1/4 inch across with a sweet, light fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded shrub with arching branches that create an elegant fountain-like shape, often broader than it is tall

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are reddish-brown and smooth, while older branches develop thin, peeling bark that feels slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small dry seed pods that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds that feel papery when crushed between fingers

habitat: In New England, Threelobe Spirea is extremely rare and typically found only where it has escaped from cultivation near old homesites or abandoned gardens. When present, it prefers well-drained soils in sunny to partially shaded locations. It may occasionally establish along woodland edges or in disturbed areas with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in mid to late spring, showing their characteristic three-lobed shape. White flower clusters bloom in late spring to early summer, attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Foliage remains green and lush throughout summer, with the three-lobed leaves being the most reliable identification feature. Flowers fade and small seed pods begin to develop.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow to orange before dropping, though fall color is often unremarkable. Seed pods mature and split open to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the arching growth pattern clearly. Reddish-brown stems and the overall fountain-like branching structure help with winter identification.

funFact: Despite being called 'Asian meadowsweet,' this shrub actually prefers drier conditions than true meadows and was once so prized in traditional Asian gardens that it was considered a symbol of elegance and refinement, often planted near meditation spaces.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other cultivated spireas, especially Bridal-wreath Spirea, but the three-lobed leaves are diagnostic - other spireas have simple, unlobed leaves. Remember: 'Three-lobe' means three-lobed leaves, not three petals or three flowers.
contextualKnowledge: This is sometimes called 'Asian meadowsweet' in the nursery trade, which can be confusing since New England has native meadowsweets (like white meadowsweet) that are completely different plants. The 'meadowsweet' name for spireas is largely historical and doesn't reflect their actual habitat preferences.
compareHints: Among New England's spireas, Threelobe Spirea is unique for its three-lobed leaves - all other regional spireas have simple, unlobed leaves. White meadowsweet has long, narrow leaves and grows in wet areas, while Steeplebush has fuzzy, oval leaves and pink flowers. The three-lobed leaves make this species unmistakable if you find it.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the meadowsweets, white meadowsweet stands out with its pure white flowers and smooth leaf undersides.
Among the Spiraea species in New England, steeplebush is the only one with distinctly pink, steeple-shaped flower clusters and woolly leaf undersides.
Japanese Spirea differs from native New England spireas like Steeplebush and White Meadowsweet by its compact, mounded garden-shrub appearance and pink flat-topped flower clusters.
Unlike the native white meadowsweet and steeplebush which have single flowers in upright cone-shaped clusters, bridal-wreath has double flowers in rounded clusters along arching branches.
Among the spireas, Reeve's stands out for its distinctly pompom-shaped flower clusters and strongly arching growth habit.
Among the spireas, Thunberg's meadowsweet stands out for its very early bloom time and fine, narrow leaves.
Northern meadowsweet is much shorter and more compact than white meadowsweet, with smaller flower clusters and a preference for cooler locations.
